summary: Hebrew adjectives have no comparative or superlative endings: you compare with words. “Bigger” is יוֹתֵר “more” + the adjective, before or after it: גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר = יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל (after is a little more formal). “Than” is the prefix מִ / מֵ, the same “from” as in lesson 11: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מֵהַדִּירָה “the house is bigger than the flat”; before a clause, an adverb or a phrase with a preposition it is מֵאֲשֶׁר (יוֹתֵר טוֹב מֵאֲשֶׁר בַּבַּיִת “better than at home”), and with a pronoun it takes endings: מִמֶּנִּי “than me”, מִמְּךָ / מִמֵּךְ “than you”, מִמֶּנּוּ “than him”, מִמֶּנָּה “than her”, מֵהֶם “than them”. “Less” is פָּחוֹת (פָּחוֹת יָקָר) and “as … as” is כְּמוֹ (גָּבֹהַּ כְּמוֹ אַבָּא). “The most” is הֲכִי before the adjective, in everyday Hebrew: הוּא הֲכִי גָּבֹהַּ “he is the tallest”, הַסֵּפֶר הֲכִי טוֹב “the best book” (the adjective then takes no article). Formal style puts בְּיוֹתֵר after a definite adjective: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל בְּיוֹתֵר “the biggest house”. The adjective itself still agrees as always (גְּבֹהָה יוֹתֵר for a woman), and there are no irregular forms: “better” is just טוֹב יוֹתֵר. Colours are ordinary adjectives that share one pattern, קָטֹל: אָדֹם → אֲדֻמָּה, אֲדֻמִּים, אֲדֻמּוֹת “red”; light and dark come after the colour and agree too (חֻלְצָה כְּחֻלָּה בְּהִירָה “a light-blue shirt”).

rows: הַמָּטוֹס הֲכִי מָהִיר. · הַסֵּפֶר הֲכִי טוֹב
blocks.caption: No comparative ending: the adjective never changes for comparison — only for gender and number.

head: than + pronoun
blocks.caption: מִ takes endings like לְ (לִי, לְךָ …): הוּא גָּבֹהַּ מִמֶּנִּי “he is taller than me”.

blocks.title: מִ is “from” and “than”
blocks.text: Arabic uses مِنْ in the same way (أَكْبَرُ مِنْ): “bigger from the flat”. Before a noun: מִ, which doubles the next letter (מִכָּאן), or מֵ before א ה ח ע ר and the article (מֵהַדִּירָה, מֵאַבָּא).

blocks.title: הֲכִי and the article
blocks.text: With הֲכִי the adjective has no article: הַסֵּפֶר הֲכִי טוֹב (not *הַסֵּפֶר הֲכִי הַטּוֹב). With בְּיוֹתֵר it has: הַסֵּפֶר הַטּוֹב בְּיוֹתֵר.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you compare
questions: Two things, one has more of the quality? → יוֹתֵר + adjective + מִ / מֵ.
The top of a group? → הֲכִי + adjective (formal: הַ… בְּיוֹתֵר).
Does the adjective still agree with its noun? → גְּבֹהָה יוֹתֵר for a woman.

askYourself: Is it “more …” (two things)? → יוֹתֵר + adjective (or adjective + יוֹתֵר).
Is there a “than”? → מִ / מֵ before a noun (מֵהַדִּירָה), מִמֶּנִּי … with a pronoun, מֵאֲשֶׁר before a clause or phrase.
Does מִ meet א ה ח ע ר or the article? → מֵ (מֵאַבָּא, מֵהַבַּיִת).
Is it “the most”? → הֲכִי + adjective, without an article on the adjective; formal: הַ + adjective + בְּיוֹתֵר.
Have I made the adjective agree with its noun?
steps: Choose the adjective and its form (gender, number).
Add the “than” part with מִ / מֵ.

traps: There is no comparative ending: “bigger” is גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר — the adjective itself does not change.
*יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל מֵאֲשֶׁר הַדִּירָה → … מֵהַדִּירָה (before a plain noun use the prefix).
“Better” is not a new word: טוֹב יוֹתֵר / יוֹתֵר טוֹב.
A light colour is בָּהִיר, not קַל (קַל is light in weight).
כָּחֹל is (darker) blue; light, sky blue is תְּכֵלֶת.

quiz.q: “The train is faster than the bus”:
quiz.why: יוֹתֵר + the adjective, which agrees with the feminine רַכֶּבֶת, + מֵ for “than”.
The prefix מִ “from” is also “than”: מֵהַדִּירָה “than the flat”.
After הֲכִי the adjective takes no article.

quiz.q: Which is formal for “the biggest house”?

quiz.why: מִ with a pronoun takes endings: מִמֶּנִּי “than me”.
The colour pattern: the last letter doubles and o becomes u.
Both the colour and בָּהִיר agree with the feminine noun; קַל is “light” in weight.

quiz.q: The fruit “orange” is תַּפּוּז. The colour orange is:
quiz.why: Hebrew has separate words: כָּתֹם (colour), תַּפּוּז (fruit).

seeAlso.note: Arabic builds a special form, the elative أَفْعَلُ (كَبِير → أَكْبَرُ), with مِنْ for “than” (أَكْبَرُ مِنْ = גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִ…, the same “from”); its colours have a pattern of their own too: أَحْمَرُ / حَمْرَاءُ / حُمْرٌ.
German changes the adjective (groß – größer – am größten) and says “than” with als; Hebrew never changes it and uses מִ. hellblau / dunkelrot = כָּחֹל בָּהִיר / אָדֹם כֵּהֶה.
Chinese also adds words instead of endings: A 比 B 大 “A is bigger than B”, 最大 “the biggest” — 比 = Hebrew מִ, 最 = הֲכִי, 更 = יוֹתֵר.

notes.text: Greek also says “than” with “from” (μεγαλύτερος από ~ גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִ…); but Greek can use an ending (-τερος), Hebrew only יוֹתֵר: גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר.

Russian uses an ending (выше) and “than” as чем or the genitive (выше брата); Hebrew uses יוֹתֵר + מִ: גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח. Russian синий / голубой are two blues; Hebrew also has two, כָּחֹל and תְּכֵלֶת.
Like más … que, Hebrew uses a word (יוֹתֵר), but “than” is מִ “from”: más grande que el piso ~ גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מֵהַדִּירָה. הֲכִי works like el más, but the adjective takes no article.
English -er / -est have no Hebrew counterpart: “bigger” is גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר, “the biggest” הֲכִי גָּדוֹל, and even “better” is just טוֹב יוֹתֵר. “Than” is מִ, the word for “from”.
plus … que ~ יוֹתֵר … מִ, le plus ~ הֲכִי; Hebrew has no irregular meilleur: “better” is טוֹב יוֹתֵר.

German uses endings (größer, am größten) and als; Hebrew uses words (יוֹתֵר, הֲכִי) and מִ “from”. Light and dark follow the colour in Hebrew (כָּחֹל בָּהִיר), where German hell- / dunkel- come before it.
Hindi also compares with “from” (भाई से लंबा “taller than the brother”); Hebrew does the same with מִ (גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח) and adds יוֹתֵר “more”.
Persian adds the ending -تر (بزرگ‌تر از …); Hebrew has no ending, only יוֹתֵר — but “than” is “from” in both: از ~ מִ.
Marathi compares with पेक्षा after the standard (भावापेक्षा उंच “taller than the brother”); Hebrew puts מִ before it and adds יוֹתֵר: גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח.
Arabic also says “than” with مِنْ, but builds a special form, the elative (أَكْبَرُ مِنْ); Hebrew has no such form — just יוֹתֵר: גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִ….
Turkish also compares with “from” and an optional “more” (evden daha büyük); Hebrew says גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מֵהַבַּיִת — the same idea, with מִ before the noun. en büyük ~ הֲכִי גָּדוֹל.
Japanese also compares with “from” (兄より高い); Hebrew says גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח and adds יוֹתֵר “more”. 一番 ~ הֲכִי.
Korean 보다 (형보다 커요) ~ Hebrew מִ (גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח); 제일 / 가장 ~ הֲכִי.
Finnish uses an ending (-mpi: isompi) and kuin or the partitive; Hebrew has no ending — יוֹתֵר + מִ.
Hungarian adds -bb (nagyobb) and uses mint or the -nál / -nél case; Hebrew uses יוֹתֵר and מִ.
Swahili uses kuliko “than” (mrefu kuliko kaka); Hebrew uses יוֹתֵר “more” and מִ “from”: גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מֵהָאָח.
Luganda compares with a verb meaning “surpass” (-singa); Hebrew uses יוֹתֵר “more” + מִ “from”.

Chinese puts 比 before the standard (他比我高) and leaves the adjective unchanged; Hebrew too leaves it unchanged, but adds יוֹתֵר and marks the standard with מִ: הוּא גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנִּי. 最 ~ הֲכִי.

Vietnamese puts hơn after the adjective (cao hơn tôi); Hebrew uses יוֹתֵר and מִ: גָּבֹהַּ יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנִּי. nhất ~ הֲכִי. And where xanh covers green and blue, Hebrew always separates יָרֹק and כָּחֹל.
Inuktitut adds a comparative suffix and puts the thing compared in the ablative case (“from”); Hebrew has no suffix, but uses מִ “from” the same way: גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מֵהַבַּיִת.
